title: Strings
description: Master text handling in Python: creating, slicing, transforming, and formatting strings

lessons.title: String Basics & Indexing
lessons.description: Create strings and access individual characters

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create strings with quotes, access characters by index, and use negative indexing.

sections.title: 📝 Creating Strings
sections.content:
Strings hold text, wrapped in single, double, or triple quotes.

```python
s1 = 'hello'
s2 = "world"
s3 = '''multi
line
string'''
```

Single and double quotes work identically — pick one and be consistent, or use double quotes when your text contains an apostrophe.

sections.title: 🔢 Indexing
sections.content:
Every character has a position, starting at 0. Negative indexes count from the end.

```python
s = "Python"
s[0]   # 'P'
s[1]   # 'y'
s[-1]  # 'n' (last character)
s[-2]  # 'o' (second to last)
```

Strings are **immutable** — you can't change a character in place; you build a new string instead.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Trying `s[0] = 'X'` to change a character — this raises a TypeError because strings can't be modified in place.

questions.question: What is `"Python"[0]`?
questions.explanation: Indexing starts at 0, so index 0 is the first character.

questions.question: What is `"Python"[-1]`?
questions.explanation: Negative index -1 refers to the last character.

questions.question: Strings in Python are...
questions.explanation: Once created, a string's characters cannot be changed in place.

questions.question: Which is a valid way to create a string?
questions.explanation: Quotes (single, double, or triple) define string literals.

questions.question: What does trying `s[0] = 'X'` do?
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable so item assignment isn't allowed.

questions.question: Triple quotes `'''...'''` are useful for...
questions.explanation: Triple quotes let a string span multiple lines.

questions.question: What is `"cat"[-2]`?
questions.explanation: Counting from the end: -1='t', -2='a'.

questions.question: Double and single quotes for strings are...
questions.explanation: Both produce the same str type in Python.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use `s[start:stop:step]` to extract parts of a string, including reversing it.

sections.title: ✂️ Basic Slicing
sections.content:
Slicing extracts a range of characters: `s[start:stop]` (stop is excluded).

```python
s = "Python"
s[0:2]   # 'Py'
s[2:]    # 'thon' (to the end)
s[:2]    # 'Py' (from the start)
s[:]     # 'Python' (full copy)
```

sections.title: ⏩ Step and Reversing
sections.content:
A third value controls the step size — negative steps go backwards.

```python
s = "Python"
s[::2]   # 'Pto' (every 2nd char)
s[::-1]  # 'nohtyP' (reversed!)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting that the `stop` index is exclusive — `s[0:2]` gives 2 characters, not 3.

questions.question: What does `"Python"[0:2]` return?
questions.explanation: Slice from index 0 up to (not including) index 2.

questions.question: How do you reverse a string s?
questions.explanation: Step -1 walks the string backwards.

questions.question: What does `s[:2]` mean?
questions.explanation: Omitting start defaults to the beginning.

questions.question: What does `s[2:]` mean?
questions.explanation: Omitting stop defaults to the end of the string.

questions.question: What is `"abcdef"[::2]`?
questions.explanation: Step 2 takes every other character starting at index 0.

questions.question: Is the stop index in a slice included?
questions.explanation: Slices are exclusive of the stop index.

questions.question: What does `s[:]` return?
questions.explanation: Omitting both start and stop copies the whole string.

questions.question: What is `"hello"[1:4]`?
questions.explanation: Characters at indices 1, 2, 3: 'e','l','l'.

lessons.title: String Methods
lessons.description: Use built-in methods to transform and inspect strings

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Apply common string methods for case, whitespace, searching, and splitting.

sections.title: 🔠 Case & Whitespace
sections.content:
```python
s = "  Hello World  "
s.strip()      # 'Hello World' (trims edges)
s.lower()      # '  hello world  '
s.upper()      # '  HELLO WORLD  '
s.title()      # '  Hello World  '
```

sections.title: 🔍 Searching & Replacing
sections.content:
```python
s = "hello world"
s.replace("world", "there")  # 'hello there'
s.find("world")               # 11 (index, or -1 if missing)
"world" in s                  # True
s.startswith("hello")         # True
s.endswith("world")           # True
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting that string methods return a *new* string — `s.upper()` doesn't change `s` itself.

questions.question: What does `"  hi  ".strip()` return?
questions.explanation: strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace.

questions.question: What does `",".join(['a','b'])` return?
questions.explanation: join() inserts the separator between list elements.

questions.question: What does `"a,b,c".split(",")` return?
questions.explanation: split() returns a list of substrings.

questions.question: Does `s.upper()` modify s in place?
options: No, it returns a new string
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable; methods return new strings.

questions.question: What does `"world" in "hello world"` return?
questions.explanation: The `in` operator checks for substring membership.

questions.question: `s.find("x")` returns -1 when...
options: x is not found in s
questions.explanation: find() returns -1 to signal 'not found'.

questions.question: What does `s.replace('a','b')` do?
options: Replaces all 'a' with 'b' in a new string
questions.explanation: replace() returns a new string with substitutions made.

questions.question: `s.startswith("he")` checks...
questions.explanation: startswith() checks the beginning of the string.

lessons.title: String Formatting
lessons.description: Build formatted strings with f-strings and .format()

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Format numbers and variables inside strings using f-strings.

sections.title: ✨ f-strings (recommended)
sections.content:
```python
name = "Sam"
price = 19.999
f"{name} paid ${price:.2f}"   # 'Sam paid $20.00'
f"{10 + 5}"                    # '15' (expressions work too)
f"{name!r}"                    # "'Sam'" (repr)
```

sections.title: 📜 .format() (older style)
sections.content:
```python
"{} is {}".format("Sam", 25)      # 'Sam is 25'
"{0} {1} {0}".format("a", "b")     # 'a b a'
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the `f` prefix and ending up with the literal text `{name}` instead of its value.

questions.question: What does `f"{3.14159:.2f}"` return?
questions.explanation: .2f formats to 2 decimal places.

questions.question: Which prefix marks an f-string?
questions.explanation: f'...' is the f-string literal prefix.

questions.question: What happens if you forget the f prefix?
questions.explanation: Without f, {name} is just text, not a substitution.

questions.question: What does `f"{42:05d}"` produce?
questions.explanation: 05d pads the integer with zeros to width 5.

questions.question: What does `"{} {}".format("a","b")` give?
questions.explanation: .format() fills placeholders in order.

questions.question: `f"{1000000:,}"` returns...
questions.explanation: , inserts thousands separators.

questions.question: Can you put expressions inside f-string braces?
questions.explanation: f-strings evaluate any valid expression inside {}.

questions.question: `f"{0.5:.0%}"` returns...
questions.explanation: % format multiplies by 100 and appends a percent sign.

lessons.title: Escape Characters & Multiline Strings
lessons.description: Include special characters and multi-line text in strings

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use escape sequences and raw/multi-line strings correctly.

sections.title: 🔣 Escape Sequences
sections.content:
A backslash introduces a special character.

```python
print("Line1\nLine2")   # newline
print("Col1\tCol2")     # tab
print("She said \"hi\"") # escaped quotes
print('It\'s here')      # escaped apostrophe
print("C:\\path\\file")  # escaped backslash
```

sections.title: 📄 Raw Strings & Multiline
sections.content:
```python
path = r"C:\path\file"   # raw string, ignores escapes

text = """This spans
multiple
lines"""
```

Raw strings (`r"..."`) are especially useful for file paths and regular expressions where backslashes shouldn't be interpreted.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to escape quotes inside a string delimited by the same quote character, or forgetting `r` before a Windows path.

questions.question: What does `\n` represent?
questions.explanation: \n inserts a line break.

questions.question: What does `\t` represent?
questions.explanation: \t inserts a horizontal tab.

questions.question: How do you write a literal backslash in a string?
questions.explanation: Doubling the backslash escapes it.

questions.question: What is a raw string used for?
questions.explanation: r'...' treats backslashes literally, useful for paths and regex.

questions.question: How do you create a raw string?
questions.explanation: r"..." is the raw string syntax.

questions.question: Triple-quoted strings are useful for...
questions.explanation: They let string literals span several lines.

questions.question: How do you include a double quote inside a double-quoted string?
questions.explanation: Backslash-escaping lets you embed the same quote character.

questions.question: What does `"It\'s"` print?
questions.explanation: The escaped apostrophe just prints as a normal apostrophe.
